content:
<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 178 would direct the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) to carry out suppression efforts for most wildfires on National Forest System lands within 24 hours of detection. Additionally, the bill would prevent the Forest Service from inhibiting suppression efforts of state or local firefighters on National Forest System lands and prohibit the Forest Service from initiating backfires or burnouts unless they are given orders from the incident commander responsible, or unless it is necessary to protect the health and safety of personnel. Lastly, the bill would limit the Forest Service's use of prescribed burns by requiring immediate suppression of fires that exceed prescription.
H.R. 178 would be a return to USFS's misguided ``10 a.m. policy'', which prioritized stomping out every fire as soon as possible--so named because it required all wildfires to be extinguished the morning after reporting. This policy for decades eliminated beneficial fire from landscapes and is widely criticized for causing the current conditions exasperating the climate-fueled wildfire crisis. According to the best available science and traditional ecological knowledge, well-managed fire on fire-evolved landscapes promotes healthy forests and reduces the frequency and severity of catastrophic wildfires. These techniques are critical to effective forest management and restoration efforts. H.R. 178 ignores this consensus by restricting the use of proven techniques and tactics for fire management.
In 2023, USFS testified in opposition to this bill, citing concerns that the legislation would reduce resource management and firefighting tools and tactics and worsen forest health. To protect firefighters, life, property, communities, infrastructure, cultural sites, watersheds, and other natural resources, the agency requires every fire to undergo a strategic risk-based response based on the threats and opportunities of the fire event's circumstances and effectively uses all current tools available to the agency. A majority of fires are suppressed, while a select few are left to burn for resource benefits or other public safety and planning reasons. Congress must prioritize supporting federal wildland firefighters and their local partners, not substitute nostalgia for the judgment and experience of the fire managers on the ground.
Furthermore, H.R. 178 is in direct conflict with the work of the congressionally authorized Wildland Fire Mitigation and Management Commission (WFMMC), which produced 148 full-consensus recommendations for how to respond to the wildfire crisis. In the report, the broad group of commission members highlighted how 20th-century fire suppression policies have resulted in unhealthy landscapes and wrote, ``policy change is needed to enable a new relationship with fire, one in which fire is no longer an existential risk to communities and landscapes, but instead an integral and beneficial component of our human and natural systems.'' Additionally, in a July 17, 2025, letter to the Committee, the organization Grassroots Wildland Firefighters characterized H.R. 178 as ``unnecessary, redundant, and . . . [a hindrance to] firefighters and managers.''
At the markup of H.R. 178, the majority adopted an Amendment in Nature of a Substitute that expanded H.R. 178 and its related fire suppression policies to cover Department of the Interior lands. Committee Democrats offered several amendments to address outstanding policy concerns, including an amendment offered by Representative Leger Fernandez that would have delayed implementation of the bill until the Forest Service has a full staff of wildland firefighters. The Forest Service has been hollowed out by the current Administration, with more than 3,000 ``red card'' fire support staff having departed the agency since January 20, 2025. Ranking Member Huffman offered an amendment to fund increased prescribed fire treatments across Forest Service lands to ensure beneficial fire still reaches fire-adapted landscapes, which was also rejected. If Congress mandates that the Forest Service carry out a full suppression policy, Congress must also ensure the agency has the staff to carry it out.
H.R. 178 would promote policies that could conflict with the best available science and even put federal wildland firefighters in harm's way. To counter the existing wildfire crisis, Congress should emphasize supporting agency capacity to build a professional workforce, not eliminating fire from the landscape. This bill is a step in the wrong direction.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
